records.our_prose: Broccoli is a cool-season brassica grown for its tight head of immature flower buds, harvested before the buds open. It performs best in the cool shoulders of spring and fall, bolts or fails to head in summer heat, and rewards a steady supply of moisture and nitrogen. After the central head is cut, most types keep producing smaller side shoots.

records.source_context: The heads of broccoli are really flower buds that must be harvested before the flowers open or show yellow. Mature heads measure 3 to 8 inches across. Smaller, lateral heads develop after the central head is cut. The spiraling heads of Romanesco broccoli are quite dramatic. Sprouting or Italian broccoli forms many florets or small heads, but do not produce a solid head.

records.our_prose: Broccoli genuinely likes a Las Vegas Valley fall: warm days ease into cool nights right as the heads size up, and that is when broccoli tastes best. Set out transplants in late winter for a quicker spring crop ahead of the summer heat, then plant again in mid-to-late summer for the fall crop many desert gardeners prefer.

records.our_prose: Up north, grow broccoli twice a year in the cooler weather at each end of the season. Plant your spring crop a couple of weeks before your last frost date so it makes heads before summer heat, and harvest starting in early summer. Then plant a second crop in mid-July for a fall harvest. The fall crop often tastes better and lasts longer because broccoli likes cool weather, and in the milder cold zones it can give you more than the spring crop. Pick fast-maturing varieties in the coldest areas, and keep a row cover handy to protect young plants from a late spring frost or an early fall one.

records.source_context: Transplants for fall planting can be produced along with cabbage and cauliflower transplants, taking about 4 to 6 weeks from seeding to setting into the garden. Seeds can be sown directly in mid-July for a fall harvest or transplants are set out by the first week in August. Fall broccoli often produces higher yields than spring plantings in the mid-Atlantic region.

records.our_prose: Cutting the central head while the buds are still tight is what triggers the side shoots, so a timely first harvest actually increases total yield. New growers often wait too long and let the head loosen or flower, which both ends the side-shoot run early and gives a coarser main head.
